hints: Notice the nucleon number stays at 13 but the proton number changes from 7 in $^{13}_{7}\text{N}$ to 6 in $^{13}_{6}\text{C}$.
A decrease in proton number by 1 means a proton has changed to a neutron inside the nucleus, which defines $\beta^+$ rather than $\beta^-$ decay.
Recall the lepton pairings: $\beta^-$ is emitted with an antineutrino $\bar{\nu}$ while $\beta^+$ is emitted with a neutrino $\nu$ to conserve lepton number.
walkthrough: Identify the numbers: $^{13}_{7}\text{N} \to ^{13}_{6}\text{C}$. Mass number $A=13$ is unchanged, proton number $Z$ changes $7 \to 6$, a decrease of 1.
A decrease in $Z$ with constant $A$ means one proton has become one neutron: $p \to n + \beta^+ + \nu$. This is $\beta^+$ decay, so eliminate options with $\beta^-$.
Check charge: left side charge $+7e$. Right side nucleus $+6e$ plus $\beta^+$ charge $+1e$ gives $+7e$, so charge is conserved.
Check lepton conservation: $\beta^+$ is an antilepton, so it must be balanced by a lepton, the electron neutrino $\nu$. An antineutrino $\bar{\nu}$ would give two antileptons.
The $\gamma$ photon carries away excess energy without changing $A$ or $Z$. Only the equation with $\beta^+ + \nu + \gamma$ satisfies all conservations. This is option D.

A.explanation: Uses $\beta^-$ but proton number falls from 7 to 6, so charge is not conserved with an electron emitted. $\beta^-$ decay would increase proton number.

B.explanation: Uses $\beta^-$ which would change a neutron to a proton and give $^{13}_{8}\text{O}$, not $^{13}_{6}\text{C}$. Proton number must decrease here.

C.explanation: Correctly uses $\beta^+$ for $7 \to 6$, but $\beta^+$ emission is accompanied by a neutrino $\nu$, not an antineutrino $\bar{\nu}$.

D.explanation: Proton number decreases by 1 so a proton becomes a neutron with $\beta^+$ emission, and $\beta^+$ decay conserves lepton number with a neutrino $\nu$.
